sub: An untested command doesn't cost you a failed unit test — it costs the university a drone. This module is the gate everything else in this course passes through.

title: One Bad Command Is All It Takes
desc: A drone has no undo, no rollback, no restore-from-backup

items: A crashed Mini 4 Pro is dead hardware and real money — the university paid for it once, and won't be happy paying twice
A flyaway is worse than a crash: the drone simply leaves and never comes back, and so does the course equipment
On a backend, a bad deploy is rolled back in minutes — a drone in a wall stays in the wall

rows: Climb velocity set with no ceiling and no stop condition — indoors it grinds into the ceiling; outdoors it climbs until the link drops and the drone is gone
Meters confused with m/s or with seconds of loop time — a wrong tick-rate assumption turns 2 m into 7 m, straight into a wall, the projector, or a person

items: Untested code never gets props. Not yours, not Claude's — no exceptions, not even for "trivial" one-liners. Especially not for those.

title: Code Flies Indoors. Outdoors, Hands Fly.
desc: The course rule on programmatic flight — and why it exists

body.card: Why outdoor + code is a different animal
items: Indoors a runaway loop meets a wall within meters — outdoors nothing stops it: the link drops, your code keeps commanding, and the drone is gone across the city
Our SDK code bypasses DJI Fly's guardrails — altitude limits and geo-zone warnings simply don't exist in your virtual-stick loop
Outdoors the drone meets uninvolved people — a code bug is no longer a lab incident, it is an aviation incident with you as the liable operator
Programmatic / virtual-stick flight happens indoors (guards on) or in the simulator. Never outdoors.
Outdoor flights are manual only: RC in hand, sticks under your fingers, following the open-category rules on the next slide
No exceptions — not for "just a quick test", not for a calm day, not for an empty field

title: Outdoors, the Law Flies With You
desc: EU open category — the rules that apply to every single outdoor flight, even under 250 g

body.card: Always — no matter how small the drone
items: VLOS: keep the aircraft in unaided sight the whole flight — not on the screen, in the sky
Max 120 m above ground — the hard ceiling of the whole open category
Geo-zones are off-limits: airports (1.5 km in Germany), hospitals, prisons, nature reserves — check DiPUL before every flight (Module 14)
Registration + insurance: operator e-ID sticker on the aircraft, liability insurance is mandatory in Germany
Never over assemblies of people, no dropping of anything, minimum age 16

body.card: Our Mini 4 Pro (C0, < 250 g) flies in A1 — the mildest class, not a free pass
items: Overflying individual uninvolved people is tolerated only if unplanned — and must be ended immediately; never plan a route over anyone
A2 (30 m distance) and A3 (150 m from built-up areas) apply to heavier drones — the full table is in Module 1
The A1/A3 certificate (EU online training + exam) is the minimum license — and it binds you personally, not the university

title: An Incident Makes You the Liable Operator
desc: Not the university. Not DJI. Not Claude. You.

items: Strict liability (LuftVG): the operator is liable for damage caused by the aircraft even without any fault — a gust, a glitch, a bug: your liability either way. That is exactly why insurance is mandatory
Rule violations — geo-zone, altitude, no VLOS — are offences with fines up to €50,000
If people are endangered, criminal law is on the table — dangerous interference with air traffic is a crime, not a fine
Insurance pays the victim — it does not protect you from fines, criminal charges, or recourse after gross negligence

body.card: What this means for you in this course
items: The person flying is personally responsible — handing you the university's drone does not move the responsibility
"The AI wrote that code" is not a defense — you armed the motors; every rule on the previous two slides exists so this slide never applies to you

title: AI-Generated Flight Code: Compiles, Looks Right, Flies Wrong
desc: Claude writes Kotlin that reads clean and builds green — the drone doesn't know that

body.card: Why AI code is uniquely risky here
items: LLM-generated code fails plausibly: it compiles, reads clean, and a quick review nods it through
On a backend, a wrong unit is a failed test — on a drone the bug has propellers; the error budget is the distance to the nearest wall
Virtual stick has no "fly 2 m" command — only velocity × time at ≥ 5 Hz. Every distance is an implicit calculation the AI can silently get wrong

body.card: The trap: letting the same AI check itself
items: If the same AI writes the code and the tests, both inherit the same wrong assumption — the tests go green and the drone still hits the wall
That is why this course demands a manual recheck of every test — you are the independent verifier the AI cannot be

title: Spot the Bug: "Fly Forward 2 m"
desc: Generated Kotlin, DJI virtual stick — it compiles, it flies, and it overshoots 3.5×

body.code: // task: "fly forward 2 m" val distance = 2.0 repeat(distance.toInt() * 5) { // "2 m at 5 Hz" — actually just 2 s of flight param.pitch = 3.5f // 3.5 m/s — copied from an SDK sample VirtualStickManager.sendVirtualStickAdvancedParam(param) delay(200L) // 5 Hz tick } // flown: 3.5 m/s × 2 s = 7 m. requested: 2 m. wall: hit.

items: Unit confusion — distance holds meters, the loop treats it as seconds; pitch is a velocity that never matched the request
No bound, no abort — nothing limits the leg length, and an exception mid-loop leaves virtual stick live with the last velocity still applied
A test written first — assertEquals(2.0, plan.distanceMeters, 0.1) — fails in milliseconds; the wall-impact version of that feedback costs a drone

title: Test Harness First, Flight Later
desc: Before any generated command flies: write the tests — then recheck the tests by hand

items: 1. Test framework first — unit tests for every distance / velocity / duration calculation before the flight code exists
2. Recheck the tests manually — read every assertion yourself and confirm the expected values against the SDK docs, not against the generated code
3. enableSimulator — fly the mission virtually and watch the telemetry: did it move 2.0 m, or 7?
4. Only then a real flight — indoors, propeller guards on, the SAFETY rules from the Lab module apply every single time
Every motion command has an explicit bound: max altitude, max distance, hard timeout
Units are visible in the code — distanceMeters, speedMetersPerSecond, durationMs — so a mix-up fails to read, not just to fly
The abort path is testable without the aircraft: the deadman timeout fires, virtual stick disables, the mission stops

title: The Gate: No Green, No Props
desc: This checklist applies to every flight, every time — there is no 'just a quick test'

items: ☐ Tests exist for every motion calculation — written before the flight code
☐ Every test manually reviewed against the SDK docs by a human
☐ Mission flown in enableSimulator — telemetry matches the intended distances
☐ Bounds, timeout and abort path verified
☐ Only then: props on, guards on, fly
This is verification independence (DO-178C, Module 3) at lab scale: the verifier must not be the author — and right now, the author is Claude
Module 11's Karate applies the same discipline to your backend: the telemetry pipeline gets tests before it gets traffic
Aviation learned this the expensive way — you get to learn it the cheap way
